item.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
item.description: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

item.title: A spectral law for blackbody radiation without temperature or Planck’s constant
Revealing Hidden Exposures: Multi-omic and Mass Spectrometry Approaches for Decoding the Chemical Exposome
item.description: Human-made chemical pollutants pose a pervasive threat to environmental and human health, yet global chemical production continues to rise while toxicological data often remains unavailable. Since regulations lag behind innovation, much of our understanding of real‑world chemical exposure frequently comes from observed biological consequences such as infertility, chronic disease, neurocognitive decline, and threats to food security. These knowledge gaps therefore illuminate major limitations in our current ability to evaluate chemical risks and highlight the need for analytical strategies capable of capturing the complexity of environmental exposures and their biological effects. The exposome provides a framework for characterizing the totality of exposures across the lifespan. Within this framework, the chemical exposome focuses specifically on exposures and effects from exogenous small molecules. Traditional targeted mass spectrometry and single-omic approaches have offered valuable but limited insights into this chemical space but often overlook co‑occurring contaminants and perturbations in interconnected molecular pathways. In contrast, multi‑omic measurements enable a more comprehensive assessment of both exposure and biological response, revealing mechanistic links between contaminants and adverse health outcomes. Developments in these areas position chemical exposomics and multi‑omics as essential tools for environmental precision health, an emerging paradigm that seeks to identify exposure‑specific molecular signatures, predict susceptibility, and guide targeted interventions. This review highlights how multi-omics, advanced analytical chemistry techniques, and sophisticated computational tools are collectively advancing a more holistic understanding of the chemical exposome.

item.title: Increasing Adhesion via Strong Dipoles: Oxazolidinone-containing Polyolefins as Nonreactive Tie Layers in Polymer Laminates
item.description: Multilayer films are widely used to combine the properties of multiple polymers but often require tie layers to achieve interfacial adhesion between the substrates. To adhere polar and nonpolar polymers, common tie layers are polyolefins containing reactive functionalities, which limit their application space and potential methods for multilayer recycling. By contrast, nonreactive tie layers require chemical modification to achieve suitable performance due to their relatively weak dipoles. To address this limitation, we synthesized a series of hydrogenated copolymers between 1,5-cyclooctadiene and an oxazolidinone-fused cyclooctene monomer (Oxa, 10–100 mol %) to form “polyethylene” functionalized with strong dipoles (~5 Debye). We tested these copolymers as nonreactive tie layers between high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and polyamide 6 (PA6), achieving adhesive strengths up to 881 N/m with moderate dipole incorporation. We observed a change in the interface of adhesive failure from PA6 to HDPE with increasing Oxa content, demonstrating a change in substrate affinity with increasing polarity. Overall, this work provides the first evidence of strong dipoles increasing interfacial adhesion for nonreactive tie layers, introducing a new adhesive design strategy for multilayer polymeric materials.

item.title: BigFingerprint: A Topology-aware Extended-connectivity Fingerprint for Polymers
item.description: Machine learning-driven polymer design and property prediction require molecular representations that encode not only local chemistry but also the statistically distributed monomer sequences and connectivity patterns and global topology that distinguish polymers from small molecules. Existing fingerprinting workflows often fail to capture global polymer architecture, as well as connectivity across repeat units, end groups, and linking groups. This work develops BigFingerprint, a topology-aware extended-connectivity fingerprint for polymers represented by BigSMILES. BigFingerprint consists of two components, a polymer extended-connectivity fingerprint, p-ECFP, that encodes atom-centered substructures within and across stochastic molecular fragments, and a polymer topology fingerprint, p-TFP, that encodes global architectural features such as block, statistical, graft, star, branched, and network topologies. Through representative structural examples and polymer property prediction tasks, BigFingerprint retains the chemical interpretability of circular fingerprints while extending their applicability to complex polymer architectures. As a critical component of the BigSMILES-centered ecosystem, BigFingerprint integrates local substructural information with global topological descriptors to provide a general and chemically interpretable representation for substructure analysis, similarity

item.title: Hierarchical Copper-Based Metal-Organic Frameworks for Improved Catalytic Performance
item.description: Introducing additional meso- or macroporosity into traditionally microporous metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) can greatly improve the catalytic performance of these materials, by reducing diffusional barriers during reactions. In this study, we demonstrate that HKUST-1 synthesized via supercritical CO2-assisted crystallization (referred to here as “scCO2-HKUST”) forms a hierarchically porous structure, combining intrinsic microporosity with newly formed macropores. X-ray diffraction (PXRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and gas sorption analyses confirmed the preservation of the crystal structure alongside macropore formation. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed a higher proportion of low-valent copper species (Cuo/Cu+) in scCO₂-HKUST compared to conventional HKUST-1, indicative of increased coordinatively unsaturated metal sites. In catalytic CO oxidation, scCO2-HKUST achieved higher conversion rates than normal HKUST-1 between 220 and 260 oC, with complete CO conversion at 260 °C versus 280 °C for the conventional sample. This enhanced activity is attributed to faster molecular diffusion through the macropores and greater accessibility of reactive copper sites.

item.title: Exploration of Particle Swarm Optimization for Parameter Identification in Phase-Field Modeling
item.description: To address the issue that phase-field (PF) simulation parameter calibration has long relied on manual experience and comparisons with static final-state results, a frame-by-frame parameter identification framework was developed. Three strategies were designed: standard Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), a hybrid PSO incorporating elitism and random reset mechanisms, and Elitist Random Search (ERS). A composite cost function was established, which combined the Dice coefficient and Chamfer distance through a weighting ratio. Hybrid PSO converged earlier and achieved a superior final global optimum cost, demonstrating that this strategy effectively mitigated the risk of entrapment in local optima. Finally, hybrid PSO went through extended validation with longer duration (15s) and larger simulation scale (400 µm × 1700 µm), the average error of the key parameters identified is approximately 2.8%. This work combined frame-by-frame dynamic comparison with hybrid PSO for PF parameter identification for the first time, fundamentally resolving the long-standing problem of degradation in this field.

item.title: The Curious Case of tBu-Cz-TPA-bis-DPPO: Lowest Structural Order Among Three Deep-Blue Hosts, Yet a Smooth Hole-Only Device Response
item.description: Deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts are compared by energy levels and photophysics, almost never by microstructure—yet order and film morphology are routinely read as proxies for how well a host will carry charge. Here three related hosts are compared from primary particles to film relief with documented, protocol-tested descriptors. The tert-butyl-substituted S3 host emerges as the least ordered on every scale: the lowest X-ray ordered fraction at every baseline setting, the shortest film correlation length at matched scan size, micrometre-scale relief and the lowest decomposition temperature, while only the S1 host shows lattice fringes. This structural disorder coexists with a smooth hole-only device response. The S3 hole-only device shows a single, nearly ideal relaxation with a capacitance close to the geometric value and an apparent hole mobility of about 5 × 10⁻⁷ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, comparable to that of the far better-ordered S1 host, although a bias-independent relaxation time is also consistent with the RC response of the layer stack. Long-range disorder in these hosts is therefore compatible with a clean hole-only response, and microstructure alone is not a reliable screen for transport.

item.title: Choosing a DFT Protocol That Ranks Deep-Blue TADF Emitters and Pairs Them with Hosts
item.description: Computational screening of deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials decides which emitters are made and which host each is paired with, yet the descriptors behind these decisions are rarely tested against measurement. We test them on 50 molecules (39 published emitters, eight references and three phosphine-oxide hosts) against measured data for 27 emitters. The range-separated ωB97X-D3 functional overestimates every singlettriplet gap (∆EST) and fails to rank the emitters because its error differs between molecular families; a family offset restores the ranking, and the global hybrids PBE0 and B3LYP rank the gaps directly (Spearman ρ = 0.59 and 0.58). Rate constants built on computed gaps are unreliable, but become accurate once the measured gap is used. For host–emitter pairing, the triplet energies of host and emitter must be computed on one footing: a calibrated host combined with as-computed emitters misclassifies almost every confined pair. A tiered, costed protocol turns these findings into selection rules for screening campaigns.

item.title: Decarboxylative radical C–C coupling of ⍺-(oxy/thio)acetic acids with electron-poor alkenes
Late-Stage Functionalization of Hydroxamic Acid Pharmaceuticals through Oxidative C-N Bond Formation
item.description: A mild, copper-catalyzed protocol is used for the oxidative activation of pharmaceuticals bearing hydroxamic acid functionalities. The aerobic dehydrogenation generates reactive nitroso intermediates that smoothly and selectively undergo trapping with olefins leading to the N-allylated products through ene-type reactions. Moreover, in presence of 1,3-dienes, [4+2]-cycloadditions provide access to bicyclic hydroxamate derivatives. The methodology is effective across a set of structurally diverse active pharmaceutical ingredients covering a broad application range from inflammation to cancer and neuromuscular diseases.

item.title: Development of a Microfluidic Droptode Sensor for Detection of Heparin in Citrated Human Plasma
item.description: Heparin, a large, negatively charged macromolecule, is an anticoagulant widely used in extracorporeal procedures. Methods to quantitate the amount of heparin in blood are therefore essential to ensure correct dosing, thus avoiding unwanted side effects such as thrombosis and hemorrhage. Electrochemical and optical methods have been developed for the detection of heparin in plasma and whole blood; however, deterioration of sensor response from matrix fouling and optical interference, respectively, are limitations of these technologies. Furthermore, methods that require minimal sample input are also desirable so as to limit consumption of blood during these procedures. Motivated by needs for a new, low volume and non-fouling clinical sensor, we developed a droplet microfluidic form of an ionophore-based optode. This method involves sub-nanoliter aqueous sample aliquots spaced by oil segments containing analyte-selective ionophore and pH-sensitive chromoionophore. Partitioning of the analyte from the aqueous droplet to the oil segment, facilitated by interactions with the ionophore, results in fluorescence changes that track with analyte concentration. Fluorescence measurements are recorded from sub-nanoliter oil segments adjacent to aqueous droplets, therefore components of the sample do not interfere with the measurement. Furthermore, reagent-conservative oil segments are continuously generated at tens of Hz in the droplet microfluidic device, eliminating the need to regenerate the oil phase for reuse. Here we report the application of this droplet optode (e.g. droptode) technology for the quantification of heparin in citrated human plasma samples over relevant clinical ranges.

item.title: A geometry-matched structure generator outperforms basin hopping for silicon cluster global optimisation at fixed relaxation budget
item.description: In cluster global optimisation the cost is dominated by local relaxations, so the number of relaxations—not wall-clock time—is the natural budget whenever each relaxation is a first-principles or machine-learned potential evaluation. We ask how much of that budget can be saved by the initial structure generator alone. We study a motif-agnostic generator that places each new atom by trilateration at a fixed bond distance from at least three alreadyplaced atoms, subject to a steric admissibility test, and we benchmark it as a drop-in initialiser for Stillinger–Weber silicon clusters with n = 24–60 atoms against three baselines: random structure search, a specialised basin-hopping implementation with single-atom, collective and surface moves and an adaptive step, and a growth-pattern beam search in the spirit of GOALS and GrowPAL. At equal relaxation budget the generator reaches lower minima than specialised basin hopping at every size from n = 32 upward, winning 8/8 paired replicates at n = 48 and n = 60 with complete distributional separation at n = 48, and it beats growth-pattern search in 7/8 paired replicates at both sizes. It also exhibits markedly lower run-to-run variance, and it was the only method to locate the deepest structure found at n = 32, n = 40 and n = 60. The advantage is absent at n = 16, marginal at n = 24, and clean from n = 32; a structural analysis of the resulting minima shows that they are more highly coordinated than the baselines’ but not more tetrahedral in bond angle, so we report the size onset as an unexplained empirical observation rather than attribute it to angular matching. We report the opposite accounting as well: because growth-pattern relaxations start from an already-optimised sub-cluster they are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper in wall-clock, and on equal CPU time the two methods are comparable, while the advantage over basin hopping persists on both accountings.

item.title: Global potential of decentralized waste biomass to solid carbon for scalable carbon removal
item.description: Livestock manure and crop residues are abundant agricultural by-products whose mismanagement releases ~1.56 Gt CO2-eq yr-1, about 22% of agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. Here, we propose a circular bioeconomy system to recover their energy, nutrients, and carbon. The proposed solar-powered, farm-scale system integrates anaerobic digestion, biomethanation, and methane pyrolysis to convert these residues into stable solid carbon, recycling hydrogen internally and returning nutrients to the soil as digestate. We apply a coupled mass, energy, and cost model globally using spatially explicit biomass and solar datasets. We estimate a sequestration potential of ~596 Mt C yr-1 (~2.2 Gt CO2-eq yr-1, ~6% of global fossil CO2 emissions), with a median levelized cost of 926 USD t-1 C for crop residue (5th–95th percentile: 904–980 USD t-1 C), and 1,534 USD t-1 C for manure (5th–95th percentile: 1,510–1,589 USD t-1 C), assuming no revenue from the carbon product. Capital expenditure dominates (~89% of cost, led by anaerobic digestion) while solar electricity contributes only ~11%. Under tailored process conditions, the product can be recovered as carbon black, graphite, carbon nanofibers, graphene, or nanotubes; both its market prices and carbon-credit prices could exceed the sequestration cost, making distributed carbon removal a potential source of farm income.

item.title: Bio-derived ionic conductive Guar Gum hydrogels as distributed circuit elements for analogue signal processing: the case of Resistor-Capacitor filters
item.description: Developing functional electronic materials from renewable resources is a key challenge toward more sustainable electronics. Here, we report on a bio-derived ionic conductive hydrogel based on guar gum and demonstrate its direct integration as a functional circuit element for analogue signal processing. Ionic conductivity is introduced by incorporating sodium chloride into the polysaccharide matrix and systematically tuned through the glycerol and salt contents. Increasing glycerol loading enhances conductivity, while varying NaCl concentration produces a non-monotonic response, with maximum conductivities in the 10-2 S cm-1 range and an optimum salt-loading window. The conductive formulation is subsequently combined with pristine guar gum, used as a dielectric, to fabricate guar gum-based resistor-capacitor elements. Their integration into low-pass and high-pass filters demonstrates frequency-selective operation in the audio range, with cut-off frequencies of 658 and 576 Hz and transition slopes of −17 and +15 dB dec-1, respectively. These results demonstrate that guar gumbased ionic hydrogels can move beyond conventional roles as substrates or electrolytes and directly perform circuit-level functions, providing a simple materials platform for low-frequency analogue electronics.

item.title: Diastereoselective synthesis of glycosyl-1-thiophosphates as reporters for nucleotide diphosphate sugar metabolism
item.description: Glycosylation controls key physiological processes such as cell-cell recognition, signal transduction, and protein folding/trafficking within subcellular compartments. Glycans are often assembled by Leloir glycosyltransferase enzymes, which use nucleotide diphosphate monosaccharides (NDP-monosaccharides) as substrates. Cells produce NDP-monosaccharides through metabolic transformation of corresponding glycosyl-1-phosphates (G1Ps). Existing LC-MS-based approaches to study NDP-monosaccharide metabolism in living cells are limited due to the mass degeneracy of the epimeric physiological pyranoses that populate the NDP-monosaccharide pool. Technology that enables tracking of NDP-monosaccharide metabolism from chemically defined metabolic precursors would illuminate these challenging-to-study pathways that are central to immunity, signal transduction, and cellular homeostasis. To circumvent this challenge, we have developed a series of cell-permeable glycosyl-1-thiophosphates (G1TPs) in which a single oxygen atom is replaced with a sulphur atom at the phosphorus centre. This chalcogen substitution generated a mass-unique signature that enabled tracking of select NDP-monosaccharide metabolites. To generate G1TPs, we leveraged a cyclic thiophosphorochloridate reagent to selectively install a 1,3,2-dioxaphospholane group at the anomeric centre of per-O-acetyl-D-pyranoses. Our approach included anomeric stereocontrol, which provided access to both native (α) and non-physiological (β) diastereomers at C1. Next, we leveraged the intrinsic strain of the dioxaphospholane system to efficiently install an S-acetyl-2-thioethyl (SATE) group by direct ring opening with thioacetate. LC-MS analysis confirmed that the resultant per-O-Ac- and SATE-protected G1TPs were cell permeable and could be deprotected to free G1TPs once inside. Importantly, metabolomic analysis revealed that an archetypal G1TP – α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate – was metabolized to the corresponding NDP-(S)-galactose in cellulo, whereas the β-counterpart was not. Finally, we demonstrated that α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate G1TP was non-toxic, did not perturb native glycan biosynthesis, and did not impact gene transcription. Combined, these results establish G1TPs as biologically silent reporters for NDP-monosaccharide metabolism.

item.title: The film, not the molecule, decides how deep-blue TADF hosts rank on gap and thermal robustness
item.description: Deep-blue host materials for thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) are usually ranked on a few molecular numbers, on the assumption that the isolated molecule anticipates the film. We test that assumption for three phosphine-oxide hosts, S1, S3 and S4, by reading protocol-locked descriptors of the dilute solution, the evaporated film, the powder and the bulk side by side, each with its uncertainty, next to a separate density-functional layer. The descriptors fall into families that rank the hosts differently: film-gap and thermal descriptors place the multi-arm S4 host first, emission and order descriptors place the compact carbazole S1 host first, and band-tail and voltammetric descriptors do not separate the two. The split appears between the molecule and the film: the two hosts emit alike as dilute molecules, yet the S4 film absorption edge lies 0.33 eV higher. Calculations validated against the measured infrared and NMR spectra show frontier levels that move far more with the functional than between hosts. Film gap and thermal robustness must therefore be measured and assessed separately from emissive quality.

item.title: How Metal-to-Linker Ratio and Concentration Govern the Nucleation Mechanism of MOF-5-inspired Crystals: Insights from Multiscale Modeling
Temperature Mediated Balance of Singlet Fission and Symmetry-Breaking Charge-Transfer in a Polycrystalline Perylene Bisimide Thin Film
item.description: Singlet fission (SF) and symmetry-breaking charge transfer (SBCT) are competing, and often concurrent, pathways observed in photoexcited organic semiconductor systems: a photoexcited molecule electronically coupled to a neighbor can yield two triplet excited states (SF) or a charge-separated radical ion pair (SBCT). The branching ratio of SF and SBCT is determined largely by the intermolecular electronic coupling, which depends on the relative orientation of neighboring molecules. In a solid thin film, this orientation is defined by the molecular packing, which is typically a static condition established during film formation, and difficult to change with external stimuli. Here, we show that intermolecular coupling in a solid thin film of an asymmetrically substituted perylene bisimide (mXPBI) can be reversibly modulated by temperature alone. Oblique π-stacking in mXPBI produces Davydov-split excitonic states with mixed Coulombic and charge-transfer (CT) coupling character. Temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction reveals modest changes in intermolecular distance and relative molecular orientation. Time-dependent density functional theory calculations demonstrate that these subtle changes to the molecular packing alter the balance between long-range Coulombic and short-range CT coupling, which is expected to influence the competition between SF and SBCT pathways. Transient absorption spectroscopy confirms this prediction, showing that the branching ratio between triplet (SF) and SBCT shifts from approximately 30:70 at 300 K to 50:50 at 100 K. These results demonstrate that excitonic coupling of mXPBI can be reversibly tuned by temperature in the solid state, thereby shifting the balance of competitive photophysical pathways.

item.title: FROST: certified Hartree–Fock limits of helium and beryllium to hundreds of significant figures
item.description: We report rigorous upper bounds on the closed-shell Hartree–Fock (HF) energies of helium and beryllium whose first 503 and 501 significant figures are correct, EHF(He) = −2.861 679 995 612 238 878 775 543 740 022 563 429 412 879 776 752 447 053 906 864 . . . Eh, EHF(Be) = −14.573 023 168 316 399 582 411 447 359 870 014 453 877 721 357 . . . Eh, against previous records of 66 and 43. The method, which we call FROST (Fock radial orbital shooting with Taylor series), uses no basis set. When every occupied orbital is an s orbital, the HF equations reduce to coupled radial differential equations for the orbitals and for one potential per pair of orbitals. We integrate them with Taylor series of order up to 873 in arbitrary-precision arithmetic, sizing every step from the local radius of convergence. The orbital energies and normalisations are fixed by nested secant shooting to a hard wall, which is the only truncation and whose error decays as e−2κR. For beryllium each orbital has its own wall, and the canonical equations are solved without enforcing exact orthogonality, which costs energy far below the wall error. The orbitals are piecewise polynomials with dyadic rational coefficients. An independent program therefore evaluates the exact determinant energy in integer arithmetic, and by the variational principle the result is an upper bound free of rounding error. The orbitals are as accurate as the energies. Their nuclear cusp is exact, and for helium the density at the nucleus and ⟨rk⟩ are obtained to about 500 significant figures (previously 32 to 65), with a pointwise error given in closed form by Whittaker functions. On a laptop, the 503-digit helium calculation takes 7.4 minutes and beryllium to 500 digits 4.0 hours. The same code gives the HF energies of H− through Ne8+ to 100 significant figures in about 15 seconds each. We locate the nearest singularities of the helium HF orbital in the complex plane at r∗ = −1.099 ± 0.577 i. This explains why single-exponent Laguerre-type bases converge sub-geometrically and predicts the optimised exponent of the previous record to within 3%. Combined with our FLAKE energy, the correlation energy of helium follows to 58 significant figures.

item.title: Thermally Induced Structural Transformation in a Two-Dimensional Conductive Metal-Organic Framework
item.description: A long-standing structural question in triphenylene-based conductive metal-organic frameworks is why closely related materials adopt either fully extended honeycomb lattices or intercalated structures containing alternating extended layers and discrete metal–ligand clusters. Ni(II)–HHTP and Co(II)–HHTP (HHTP = 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene) have both been reported to have the latter “intercalated structure”, but here we discover that thermal activation and dehydration convert both frameworks to the fully extended structures. Focusing on Ni(II)–HHTP, we show that this structural transformation is reversible, with roomtemperature hydration restoring the intercalated structure. Variable-temperature synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction supports the intercalated-to-fully-extended structural transformation, while solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, thermal analysis, and elemental analysis provide evidence for the accompanying dehydration. Rehydration of Ni(II)–HHTP restores the intercalated structure, establishing reversible structural switching through removal and reincorporation of water. The resulting change in interlayer architecture alters electrical conductivity, gas response and adsorption properties in Ni(II)–HHTP. Importantly, common sample pre-treatment and testing conditions can themselves change the type of framework structure, meaning that measured properties may not correspond to the initially assigned structure. Because thermal and hydration history determine structure and function, careful structural verification under measurement conditions is, therefore, essential for establishing reliable structure–property relationships. Ultimately our findings resolve a persistent structural ambiguity in this family of materials and allow access to new fully extended electrically conductive framework materials.

item.title: Polarization-Driven Hydride Transfer Promotes Cobalt Tetrasulfophthalocyanine-Catalyzed Hydrogen Evolution by Five Orders of Magnitude
item.description: The hydricity of M–H intermediates is a key descriptor and optimization target for the rational design of molecular hydrogen evolution electrocatalysts. Adsorption to an electrode surface is known to augment catalytic rate, but it remains unclear how adsorption affects M-H hydricity. Herein, we quantitatively compare the catalytic activity and mechanism of the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) from cobalt tetrasulfophthalocyanine (CoTSPc) in a dissolved aqueous form (CoTSPc(aq)) and when adsorbed to the surface of a carbon electrode (CoTSPc/C). At the same electrode potential, CoTSPc/C catalyzes HER at a rate that is over five orders of magnitude faster than CoTSPc(aq). Mechanistic studies indicate that both CoTSPc/C and CoTSPc(aq) catalyze HER via a rate-limiting hydride transfer to a proton donor in solution to form H2. Hydride transfer from Co-H in CoTSPc(aq) is a purely chemical step defined by a constant hydricity of 22.4 kcal mol−1 that is independent of applied potential. In contrast, hydride transfer from Co-H in CoTSPc/C is strongly polarization dependent, decreasing hydricity by ~23 kcal mol−1 V−1 to values as low as 1.2 kcal mol−1 at −1.1 V vs SHE, leading to the observed rate promotion. We attribute this mechanistic change to the positioning of the CoTSPc-H intermediate within the electrochemical double layer, such that the hydride traverses the interfacial electrostatic potential difference during the RLS. These results demonstrate the power of surface adsorption to generate highly reactive molecular hydrides and fundamentally reshape the free energy landscape of electrocatalysis.

item.title: Inhibiting LINE-1 retrotransposons therapeutically in disease
item.description: The LINE-1 retrotransposon is a virus-like genomic element that can activate in diseased cells. It has been implicated in cancer, autoimmunity, developmental disorders, infectious disease and neurodegeneration. LINE-1 can be inhibited by reverse transcriptase inhibitors, small molecules originally developed for HIV. The correlation between HIV and LINE-1 inhibition is ∼0.9 on a log scale, in spite of >450 Mya of evolutionary history since retroviruses diverged from retrotransposons. Suppression of HIV requires prevention of a completed 9.7 kb virus insertion into the genome in immune cells. However, every cell in the body already contains >100 copies of LINE-1 that can potentially activate. Even incomplete LINE-1 mediated insertions can cause damaging mutations and genome instability. Furthermore, partial HIV and LINE-1 products in the cytoplasm of cells can contribute to an inflammatory immune response. Preclinical studies have shown LINE-1 inhibitors slow the progression of otherwise unrelated diseases. LINE-1’s contribution to these diseases can potentially be quantified using single-nucleus whole-genome sequencing on diseased tissue, enabling prioritization of disease selection for therapeutic development. Furthermore, LINE-1’s ORF1p protein can be measured in the blood of individuals with certain cancers. LINE-1 inhibitors could therefore be extended to various diseases. Potentially used both as an anti-inflammatory and prophylactically to help preserve genome integrity. Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are available at low cost for HIV, and higher doses of some could be used to inhibit LINE-1. However, reverse transcriptase inhibitors do not prevent DNA cutting by LINE-1’s endonuclease. Novel inhibitors may therefore be required. This, combined with novel diagnostics opens up possibilities for inhibiting LINE-1 therapeutically in disease

item.title: Folding and Function as Two Sides of One Coin: Statistical Mechanics, Information Theory, and Deep Learning of Binding, Catalysis, and Allostery in an Exactly Enumerable Lattice Protein
item.description: Folding and function depend on the same conformational ensemble, but they need not favor the same population distribution. We examine this relationship in a 27-residue lattice protein with 103,346 exactly enumerated compact conformations, combining statistical mechanics, information-theoretic analysis, and variational autoencoders. Exact identities separate binding into native-site recognition and population terms, distinguish transition-state complementarity from reorganization in catalysis, and express allosteric coupling as a conformational covariance. Under composition-conserving selection, binding and turnover optimization favor a dominant compact fold, whereas strong allostery can coexist with a distributed ensemble: pure coupling optimization gives a median native population of 0.47, compared with 0.85 when designs with additional stability rewards are pooled. Composition-free binding and catalytic selection provide further counterexamples to an unconditional function-to-folding implication. Rényi divergences quantify the shortfall from the best available binding or transition-state-recognition conformation; allosteric coupling instead depends on the magnitude and alignment of two ligand-induced responses. A sequence VAE generates target-fold-compatible sequences more frequently than an independent-site baseline and partially retains binding and catalytic properties, but not allosteric coupling. Time-lagged VAEs resolve additional basin information in selected allosteric trajectories, although incomplete interconversion prevents inference of equilibrium switching kinetics. Together, these results identify a conditional relationship between functional selection and fold specificity, and distinguish population concentration for recognition from population redistribution for allosteric communication.

item.title: Volumetric self-assembly of addressable DNA frames
item.description: The ability to organize distinct molecular components at prescribed positions throughout a three-dimensional volume remains a central challenge in programmable self-assembly. Although DNA nanotechnology has enabled both highly addressable structures and assemblies of considerable size, combining these capabilities is limited by the growing number of unintended interactions between components. Here, we develop a sequence-encoded strategy for the volumetric assembly of uniquely addressed DNA origami cubes. Each cube carries 24 programmable address codes that determine its position through cooperative interactions with neighboring cubes. We formulate address generation as a coding problem, derive its theoretical capacity and develop computational methods to identify and suppress incorrect multivalent binding configurations. Using this approach, we assemble a range of three-dimensional architectures, including a 6 × 6 × 6 cuboid that contains 216 unique cubes, spans 300 nm and is encoded by a single scaffold and 361 distinct oligonucleotides. We further demonstrate site-specific organization of 18-nm gold nanoparticles into prescribed three-dimensional patterns and use single-molecule DNA-PAINT to resolve spatially encoded features at the level of individual cubes. These results establish a framework for large-scale volumetric self-assembly in which molecular identity, spatial position and cargo placement can be independently programmed, providing a route toward aperiodic nanomaterials with designed three-dimensional organization.

item.title: Exciton Diffusion Drives Efficiency Roll-off in TADF OLEDs
item.description: 2 Abstract Despite their potential to deliver high-efficiency organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), those using thermally activated delayed fluorescent (TADF) emitters often suffer from a large drop in efficiency at high luminance. This effect is known as efficiency roll-off and is a longstanding issue for these devices, which has limited their commercial deployment. We have discovered that the degree of overlap between the photoluminescence (PL) and absorption spectra drives singlet exciton diffusion and is a strong predictor of the magnitude of efficiency roll-off in TADF OLEDs. This effect is especially important in OLEDs made with multiresonant (MR)-TADF materials given their intense low-energy short-range charge transfer absorption bands. MR-TADF OLEDs are very appealing due to their narrow emission spectra; however, their small Stokes shift leads to large spectral overlap and contributes to these devices showing severe efficiency roll-off. Developing TADF materials that have a larger Stokes shift whilst maintaining their bright, narrow emission would help minimize efficiency roll-off while securing high internal quantum efficiencies, features particularly relevant for displays.

item.title: Thermal expansion of the Martian mineral starkeyite (MgSO4·4H2O) and the effect of synchrotron X-ray radiation damage on its lattice parameters
item.description: Starkeyite, MgSO4·4H2O, is one of the few hydrated sulfate minerals identified by X-ray diffraction on the martian surface, yet its structure and lattice parameters are known only at room temperature, whereas the material is exposed to much colder conditions on the surface of Mars. We report the crystal structure of perdeuterated starkeyite at 10 K and 300 K from high-resolution neutron powder diffraction, including freely refined deuterium positions, and its lattice parameters over 10–370 K, providing the first reference data for this mineral across the full Martian temperature range. Thermal expansion is strongly anisotropic and near-uniaxial, with α1 : α2 : α3 = −0.12(4) : 0.89(5) : 1.00 at 305 K and the negative direction lying in the ac plane; the volume expansion is identical within uncertainty to that of the polymorph cranswickite despite their different topologies. At ~245 K, a temperature crossed daily at the surface of Gale crater on Mars a shoulder emerges on the 212 reflection that cannot be accounted for by the P21/n model, possibly indicating a hitherto unrecognised low-temperature modification. A synchrotron X-ray experiment on protiated starkeyite yields lattice parameters that diverge progressively from the neutron data, show cooling–heating hysteresis and negative expansion of the a-axis; snapshot patterns on irradiated and fresh sections of the capillary demonstrate that this is due to radiation damage. We describe the radiation-induced strain by a second-rank X-ray expansion tensor rij which in starkeyite is strongly anisotropic, reaches a volumetric value of 11.8 TGy-1 at an absorbed dose of 0.39 GGy, and largely anneals out on reheating to room temperature. Such doses cannot be reached on Mars, but they are routinely exceeded in synchrotron studies of minerals, where radiationinduced strain is indistinguishable from the thermal or pressure response within a single dataset and can bias lattice parameters, V–T relations and equation-of-state fits, particularly for hydrates and other beam-sensitive phases and in diamond-anvil-cell experiments where the sample cannot be moved to a fresh spot. We recommend that dose be recorded as a routine experimental variable and that thermal expansion be cross-checked against neutron or low-flux reference data.

item.title: Structure – Stability Relationships in Aryl- and Heteroarylmethanesulfonyl Chlorides and Fluorides
item.description: Sulfonyl chlorides are among the most widely used yet least storable building blocks in medicinal chemistry, and arylmethanesulfonyl chlorides in particular remain poorly represented in commercial catalogs because of their limited stability. In this work, the long-term stability of 23 aryl- and 36 heteroarylmethanesulfonyl chlorides and fluorides was evaluated systematically. Decomposition was monitored by 1H NMR spectroscopy in THF-d8 solution at 4 °C and 23 °C for up to 12 months; the solvent was chosen to avoid solvolysis and acidic admixtures, and to minimize water uptake. Whereas at least one batch of each compound remained unchanged in neat form for up to 14 years (median 5.5 years), their stability in solution varied widely, i.e., from complete decomposition of a pyridine derivative within one month to no detectable change over more than 12 months, and was governed by both the electronic nature and the position of the substituent. Notably, both strongly electron-withdrawing and strongly electron-donating substituents proved destabilizing, and the decomposition products differed accordingly: sulfonic acids for electron-poor and benzyl chlorides for electron-rich substrates. Sulfonyl fluorides proved considerably more robust: all heteroaromatic derivatives studied, except isothiazole (8% after 12 months) and pyridine (15% within one week), showed no detectable decomposition over 12 months. We believe that the resulting stability map, which assigns each compound to a defined storage class, will make arylmethanesulfonyl halides practical building blocks for early drug discovery in the near future.

item.title: Charged Interface in Battery Breaks Molecular Chiral Symmetry
item.description: Molecular events occurring within a few solvent layers at a charged electrode surface govern the rate and reversibility of reactions in electrochemical devices, yet such interfacial mechanism was never sufficiently understood at atomistic-level. Here we report a counter-intuitive discovery that charged interface breaks down the mirror symmetry between R- and S-enantiomers of propylene carbonate (PC), which expresses at graphite surface into distinct interphasial chemistries. Using enantiopure R- and S-PC as a chemically identical model pair against their racemic mixture, we find interphase at graphite diverges sharply at high lithium salt concentration, where R-PC enables reversible graphite lithiation with a LiF-rich interphase, while S-PC exfoliates graphite. Simulations and spectroscopies identify the combination of high salt concentration and charged interface collectively responsible for inducing the collapse of enantiomerism into diastereomerism. This knowledge not only establishes a hitherto-unknown dimension for electrolyte design, but also introduces a new concept of broad implications beyond battery applications.

item.title: Metal Nanocluster-Based Metal-Organic Frameworks for Catalysis
item.description: 2 Metal nanoclusters (MNCs) are a class of ultrafine metal nanoparticles, comprising several metal atoms that possess distinctive electronic and geometric structures. In addition to these intrinsic properties, MNCs have various structural parameters that can be precisely tuned, such as the number of constituent atoms, geometric configuration, and heteroatom doping with other metal species. Because MNCs exhibit unique catalytic performance that is highly dependent on these structural factors, their synthesis and application in catalysis have been actively investigated in recent years. Notably, metal nanocluster-based metal-organic frameworks (MNC-MOFs) have emerged as a novel class of porous crystalline nanomaterials. These frameworks not only retain the unique characteristics of the parent MNCs that serve as their secondary building units but also acquire enhanced structural stability and additional functionalities derived from the bridging organic linkers. In this review, we summarize the catalytic performance of MNC-MOFs and discuss the outlook of this rapidly developing research field.

item.title: Photoinduced C–S Cleavage in Thiols and Oligopeptides to Initiate Controlled Radical Polymerization
item.description: Conjugating synthetic polymers to therapeutic peptides is a powerful strategy to improve their stability and enable less frequent dosing. While numerous methods have broadened the chemical space of accessible polymers, many rely on multi-step syntheses that reduce the overall yield of the final conjugate. Herein, we report a user-friendly, photocatalyst-free method to initiate polymerization via photoinduced cleavage of C–S bonds in native cysteine residues, coupled with reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymerization. Under optimized conditions, a variety of acrylate and acrylamide monomers underwent controlled polymerization from monomeric cysteine units and unprotected (oligo)peptides. We also extended this method to initiate polymerization from other thiol-containing small molecules, including those that yield non-stabilized C-centered radicals. The resulting polymers have narrow mass distributions, good agreement between theoretical and experimental molar masses, and exceptionally high α-chain-end fidelities (>99%). Collectively, these results establish an efficient, selective approach to initiating controlled radical polymerization via C–S cleavage, which can be broadly applied to designing peptide-polymer conjugates and other functional composite materials.

item.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation
item.description: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.

item.title: Phosphorus-Mediated Optical Defect Engineering in Single-walled Carbon Nanotubes
item.description: Defect engineering of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) offers a versatile strategy for tailoring their optical properties through localized chemical modification. However, expanding the range of accessible defect chemistries beyond established oxygen- and aryl-based functionalities remains an important challenge. Here, we report a straightforward, light-driven strategy for introducing phosphorus-derived defects into (6,5)-enriched SWCNTs using triphenylphosphine (TPP) and a photosensitizing dye. Ultraviolet irradiation in the presence of TPP and eosin Y generates a new near-infrared emission feature centered at 1125 nm, assigned to a defect-associated emissive state (E11*), alongside the intrinsic nanotube emission at 997 nm. The formation of this state depends on the TPP concentration, photosensitizer concentration, and irradiation time, and is accompanied by attenuation of the intrinsic optical transition and an increase in the Raman D/G intensity ratio, indicating progressive structural modification of the nanotube framework. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals a phosphorus-associated chemical state and changes in the carbon chemical environment, supporting phosphorus incorporation and the formation of modified carbon sites. Control experiments further demonstrate that defect formation requires both photosensitization and irradiation, is enhanced under oxygen-depleted conditions, and is suppressed by radical scavenging, consistent with a radical-mediated photochemical pathway. Complementary density functional theory calculations support the formation of a covalent carbon–phosphorus bond, accompanied by a change in phosphorus coordination from three- to four-coordinate, and reveal a phosphorus-associated electronic trap state near the valence-band edge. These findings establish phosphorus-mediated defect engineering as a complementary approach to tailoring SWCNT optical properties and provide a foundation for investigating the relationships between defect chemistry, localized electronic states, and near-infrared emission.

item.title: A spectral law for blackbody radiation without temperature or Planck’s constant
item.description: Planck introduced the constant h in 1900 to fit the blackbody spectrum but for years questioned whether it implied that energy is quantized or was merely a feature of its mathematical description. Here we show that his reservation was justified. The shape of the spectrum is determined by a single measured spectral rate, either its peak frequency νmax or its spectral width D, the rate at which the radiation loses phase correlation (its decoherence rate). Their ratio, D/νmax = 4.7368, is a dimensionless constant of the blackbody, internal to its spectrum. The shape follows from two relations among frequencies: the profile is a sum over integer harmonics of each frequency, as required for a recurrence rate, and each harmonic is weighted exponentially in its own frequency on the scale of D. The measured spectrum thus contains the structure needed to predict itself. A mathematical control without the recurrence constraint returns the Rayleigh–Jeans limit. On the COBE/FIRAS spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), the measured width alone predicts the shape with no fitted parameter, to a median absolute error of 0.005% of the maximum intensity, and the peak frequency νmax to 0.03%. A width–temperature calibration recovers the CMB temperature to 0.01%. Beyond spectral shape, a second spectral constant , governs the fourth-power relation between integrated intensity (I) and decoherence rate. Mapping the intensity–decoherence relation into temperature recovers the Stefan–Boltzmann constant 𝜎. The constants h, kB (Boltzmann’s constant) and 𝜎 appear only when the measured spectral relations are expressed in terms of temperature, energy, or absolute radiance, quantities assigned from outside the spectrum. The variable of the blackbody is therefore its coherence, not its temperature: for blackbody radiation, temperature is the decoherence rate expressed in kelvin. For other thermal radiation the two separate: structured thermal emitters at the same temperature emit with decoherence rates 7 to 150 times below the blackbody value. The discreteness the blackbody spectrum requires is the integer order of harmonics, a relation among frequencies, and not quantized energy.

item.title: Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry: Accumulation and Self-Improving Memory Mechanisms for Polymer Research
item.description: Memory systems for AI agents are a valuable component of long-running workflows. They are also a strong form of lock-in for model providers, because the memory system that makes a model better with use may be inaccesible to users. An ideal memory system would accumulate both factual knowledge and the relationships of that knowledge to recurring tasks performed by the researcher. People accumulate particular and general knowledge through experience, the latter often through periodic reflection on what is working and isn’t working at a higher level of abstraction. Here, we introduce an open-source harness for polymer research meant to heuristically mimic (i) knowledge accumulation across research tasks, (ii) the review of new knowledge against existing knowledge, and (iii) performing periodic updates to task-knowledge relationships through reflection. The system, which we call the Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry (OOPC, pronounced ‘oopsie’), is initialized with a knowledge base consisting of an open-source wikipedia with entries for most known polymers. From this starting point, the knowledge base was enriched by running a 1,092 task campaign across different areas of polymer chemistry, producing 8,899 distinct findings extracted from 1,679 sources on 157 different polymers. GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 comparisons were run with and without the accumulated memory from this campaign on 60 held-out tasks with varying overlap in terms of polymer and properties being researched. The performance improvements tracked with research topic similarity to prior work researched from the harness, with token reductions of up to 19% and 48% and web search reductions of up to 80% and 72% (10.3 to 2.1 and 7.6 to 2.1 per answer) for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, respectively. The harness was tested through five independent restarts of 500 tasks each with reproducible performance gains. An independent review of the performance caught rare contradictory claims and occasionally unsubstantiated claims depending on the underlying model (up to a few percent of all claims by claude on withheld tasks, none by codex). The reflection heuristic was tested as an update to the knowledge ontology after the accumulation period. These updates mainly consisted of extended lists of property names with marginal improvements to finding recall. The roles of review and ontology updates require further study as after knowledge accumulation these tests had little room to show appreciable gains given the consistently strong evidentiary basis for findings within the harness. Looking forward, domain-specific memory systems are likely to be valuable and ideally transferable research artifacts that can be shared at the group, community, and organizational levels.

item.title: Ni/TiO2 Interfaces Enhance Benzaldehyde Selectivity in the Photocatalytic Dehydrogenation of Benzyl Alcohol
item.description: The selective conversion of alcohols to carbonyls (ketones and aldehydes) plays an important role in chemical manufacturing. Photocatalytic acceptorless dehydrogenation offers a light-driven alternative for producing value-added aldehydes and H2 under mild conditions and with easy separation and high molar efficiency. However, using semiconductor photocatalysts to achieve high selectivity and long-term stability under prolonged high-intensity illumination remains challenging. In this work, we developed CdS/TiO2/Ni photocatalysts by depositing TiO2 onto CdS nanoparticle panels via atomic layer deposition (ALD), followed by Ni cocatalyst photodeposition, for the acceptorless dehydrogenation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde and H2. Diluting the benzyl alcohol concentration to a practical range of ~10 vol% (1 M) further increased benzaldehyde selectivity to ~95%. Ni photodeposition and zeta-potential measurements suggest that TiO2 coatings progressively modify Cd2+-associated surface sites through Ti3+/Ti4+ incorporation, altering adsorption kinetics and contributing to the reduced activity. This extends the photocatalyst’s lifespan from ~23 to 60 hours and increases cumulative benzaldehyde and H2 production. TiO2 thin-film coatings have emerged as a promising strategy to protect semiconductor photocatalysts while modifying surface active sites and reaction kinetics, and their stability-activity trade-off showing lower initial-stage activity beyond 15-cycle ALD will be discussed alongside proposed mechanisms. This work establishes a semiconductor/coating/cocatalyst design architecture that highlights the importance of engineering surface adsorption and active-site environments, alongside charge-separation strategies based on band-edge energetics and charge-carrier dynamics, to jointly optimize photocatalytic activity and product selectivity for targeted chemical synthesis.

item.title: Interaction without an interaction module
item.description: The prevailing way to model a many-body system is to encode every component and then let a module capture interaction. We show that the explicit interaction module is harmful when the number of components increases. We use a simple plastic encoder that compresses a component’s interaction contribution into its representation, and combine the representations by linear aggregation. This modelling approach is simple in form yet delivers unexpectedly excellent performance: it matches the prevailing explicit route under most conditions and exceeds it when a mixture carries more components than the training set covered. Moreover, an encoder produced this way has a clear advantage over per-component descriptors when it is transferred to a similar task: it greatly reduces the data requirements.

item.title: The study of secondary isotope substitutions on adjacent carbon atoms affecting the tunnelling rate in acetylacetone
item.description: Heavy-atom isotope effects on hydrogen-tunnelling splittings have been reported for malonaldehyde and tropolone but not for acetylacetone, where the splitting has not yet been measured. We predict the effects of 13C substitution at positions not directly attached to the transferring proton on its tunnelling splitting. The model is a relaxed one-dimensional reaction path on a semiempirical GFN2-xTB surface that is scaled to the coupled-cluster barrier, with the parent splitting fixed by a diffusion Monte Carlo calculation. It is tested against instanton calculations and the experimental 13C effects in malonaldehyde, and against a fulldimensional ring-polymer instanton calculation for acetylacetone on the same GFN2-xTB potential energy surface, free of the model’s fitted parameter. Substitution of 13C at both carbons bonded to the oxygens decreases the splitting by 2.1% (model range 1.5–2.5%; instanton 2.3%), and a single oxygen-bonded 13C by 1.1%. The central-and methyl-carbon isotope effects are not established. These two oxygen-bonded carbons move with the proton during tunnelling, but the instanton fluctuation prefactor cancels about a third of this kinematic effect. In malonaldehyde the model reproduces the instanton results for substitution at the oxygen-bonded carbons and the measured total effect for all three carbons, although the only positionresolved measurement gives about half as much for the oxygen-bonded pair. Predicted shifts of 0.69 cm−1 (20.5 GHz) for 2,4-13C2-acetylacetone and about half that for the naturally abundant singly labelled species present an experimental test.

item.title: Computational Exploration of Dopamine Adsorption on Carbon Nanotubes for Electrochemical Sensing
item.description: Dopamine (DA), has a variety of impacts on human health. Due to the high cost and labor-intensity of its current measurement methods, sensitive and low-cost electrochemical sensors with carbonaceous substrate materials have been proposed as an alternative. Single-chirality single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) have gained interest for their chirality-dependent properties. In a recent study, we demonstrated that the sensing response of DA varies for SWCNT chiralities. In this study, we performed density-functional theory (DFT) simulations to identify low-energy conformers of DA and to gain atomic-level understanding of the interactions upon DA adsorption on (6,6) SWCNTs. We utilized Bayesian Optimization Structure Search (BOSS) to sample energy landscapes and identify the lowest-energy DA conformers and adsorption configurations. As a result, we found 6 low-energy conformers of DA and one adsorption configuration type of DA on the (6,6) SWCNT, where the aromatic ring of DA adsorbs flat on the SWCNT and the flexible side chain is oriented away from the substrate. Analysis of its electronic structure revealed that DA physisorbs on the (6,6) SWCNT via the aromatic ring. The present workflow can be expanded to other chiralities and molecules to support substrate material development for electrochemical sensors with applications in healthcare and environmental monitoring.

item.title: Comparative Analysis of Basic Machine Learning and Rigorous Free-Energy Calculation on Benchmarking Datasets of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
item.description: Rigorous free-energy methods based on molecular dynamics simulations like free-energy perturbation (FEP) are nowadays widely applied in lead optimization in pharmaceutical companies. Due to sampling restrictions and potential force-field deficiencies, it is common practice to first validate the applicability of FEP to a target/chemical series using a small number of known compounds, before applying it prospectively. As rigorous methods require significant computational resources, we want to explore how basic machine learning (ML) methods perform under the same conditions, i.e., training on a small number of known compounds and estimating the affinity of novel variants in the same chemical series. We apply classical ML models using 2D and 3D molecular descriptors, alongside two implementations of 3D quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, and integrate the predictions through meta-learning. For many of the standard benchmarking datasets, we find that one of the ML models matches or exceeds the performance of FEP. Interestingly, ML-based predictions generally exhibit flatter slopes in parity plots, but without substantial effect on the relative rank ordering of compounds. Given their lower computational cost and ease of deployment, basic ML methods, particularly the meta-learner, emerge as a powerful complement to rigorous free-energy methods for estimating binding affinities within chemical series.

item.title: Dynamics of oxygen and hydrogen species at the surface Ru/Al2O3 revealed by advanced operando spectroscopies
item.description: The microscopic evolution of supported Ru-oxide nanoparticles under reducing conditions remains a central challenge in hydrogenation catalysis. In 5 wt% Ru/Al2O3 catalyst, the transformation of oxidized Ru species into metallic Ru, the formation of hydrides, and hydrogen exchange with the support are closely related but difficult to resolve simultaneously. Here, operando IR and O K-edge NEXAFS, supported by quantum chemical DFT calculations, show that the initially hydroxylated Ru-oxide surface contains *OOH and *OO-H species at unsaturated Ru sites characterized by a distinct O K-edge electronic signature. Upon dehydration, removal of neighboring surface groups strongly stabilizes a bridged η2-peroxo species with a characteristic vibrational fingerprint. Subsequent exposure to H2 drives a low-temperature multistep reduction to metallic Ru and leads to the transient formation of terminal Ru–H species. Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements independently reveal multi-coordinated hydrides under hydrogen-rich conditions, while H/D isotope exchange shows reversible hydrogen exchange between Ru nanoparticles and the support. The concomitant recovery of alumina hydroxyl groups upon H2 exposure further supports hydrogen transfer to the support. These results provide insight on the evolution of the catalyst, showing that surface dehydroxylation, Ru-oxide reduction, hydride formation, and hydrogen transfer are closely connected during activation of Ru/Al2O3 catalysts.
