Three distinct regimes emerge: the V-series requires a special-cubic model with a dominant ternary Y2O3·ZnO·CeO2 term (β = −47.2, p = 0.001; R2(pred) = 97 %); the T-series is strictly linear (R2(pred) = 55 %), higher orders overfitting; and both La-series show a significant La2O3·CeO2 interaction absent in their Y-analogues. Three additive property models (Makishima–Mackenzie, an extended variant, and Yamane–Sakaino) deviate systematically from measured spE (absolute errors 6.9–12.2 × 106 N·m·kg-1, negative R2), most strongly where DoE detects interactions. The study delineates where additive approaches suffice, where binary synergy dominates, and where genuinely ternary cooperative effects must be resolved.

item.title: Electronic Descriptors Lower Oxygen-Vacancy Formation-Energy Error Relative to Crystal Structure Alone in Non-Magnetic Oxides
item.description: Oxygen vacancies control conduction, catalysis and ion transport in oxides, and an error of 0.3 eV in their neutral formation energy changes their concentration at 1000 K thirty-fold. Graph networks predict this energy from structure alone, but whether electronic descriptors of the pristine host from density-functional theory help is untested at matched training oxides. We compared a structure-only network (S) with one also given 22 such descriptors (D) on 1726 vacancy sites in 818 non-magnetic oxides of the Kumagai database, testing on unseen formulas. S reached 0.297 eV, the published accuracy. With 654 training oxides and equal tuning, D lowered the site error by 0.033 [0.021, 0.045] eV (95% interval), inside a 0.05 eV tolerance (1.8-fold in concentration). Tuned alone in a wider search, D* gained 0.069 [0.060, 0.078] eV, above it, but 0.039 [0.030, 0.048] eV over default-initialised S. The descriptors remove 11 to 23% of the error of S, depending on tuning. Within oxides the gain is concentrated in hosts whose cations have an empty valence s shell: empty-shell post-transition hosts gain 0.075 [0.050, 0.102] eV more than lone-pair hosts. Descriptors predicted from structure never surpass S, so the gain requires computed descriptors; where these are unavailable, S suffices for neutral vacancies.

item.title: One-Electron Modulation of Photophysics in a Through-Space Donor–Acceptor System
item.description: Through-space donor–acceptor interactions provide an attractive strategy for controlling molecular electronic structures and excited-state properties. However, the influence of one-electron transformations on the photophysical behavior of such systems remains relatively unexplored. Herein, we report an isolable carbazole–xanthylium cation (5+) and its corresponding neutral radical (5•), in which the donor and acceptor units are held in close spatial proximity. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals short donor–acceptor contacts of approximately 3.37 and 3.45 Å for the cation and radical, respectively. The cation exhibits a broad nearinfrared absorption extending to approximately 930 nm, whereas one-electron reduction affords a neutral radical displaying visible absorption and red photoluminescence with a quantum yield of 3.7 %. Density functional theory calculations and natural transition orbital analyses reveal pronounced through-space charge-transfer (TSCT) character in both species, despite their substantially different excitation energies. Excited-state geometry optimizations further support the distinct energetic landscapes associated with their charge-transfer excited states. These findings demonstrate that one-electron reduction can substantially modulate the photophysical properties of a spatially confined donor–acceptor system while preserving its underlying TSCT character.

item.title: Cellulosic fibers coated in mineral sheaths for flame-retardant nonwovens
item.description: While plant-based materials composed of cellulosic fibers have a favorable sustainability profile in several respects compared to synthetic alternatives, they are flammable and often require treatment for safe use. Many traditional flame-retardant finishes are toxic, while others are difficult to integrate with fibers or fabrics. In this work, cellulosic fibers (cotton, lyocell, jute, and hemp) were coated with crystalline calcite (calcium carbonate) or gypsum (calcium sulfate dihydrate) using a “polymer-induced liquid precursor” strategy. During this process, supersaturated solutions of insoluble minerals are induced by additives to form metastable intermediate droplets before crystallizing. These droplets wet the fibers via capillary action before nucleating to form crystalline sheaths that surround the fibers; calcite coatings were notably smooth and conformal, whereas gypsum coatings were faceted and less durable. Following mineralization, fibers were assembled into nonwoven sheets using carding/needlepunching or wetlaid techniques, then subjected to flame testing. While unmineralized cellulosic nonwovens burned readily, most nonwovens derived some degree of flame-retardancy from the mineral coatings, which serve as a heat/mass transfer barrier hindering flame propagation; further, gypsum endothermically loses its waters of hydration at low temperatures. Most mineralized nonwovens either self-extinguished or were consumed very slowly by the propagation of a flameless smoldering front.

item.title: Polariton-Mediated Electron Transfer Rate Constant from Non-Equilibrium Fermi’s Golden Rule
item.description: We provide a time-domain derivation of the population transfer rates for the polariton-mediated electron transfer (PMET) reaction under the collective coupling regime. Our theoretical analysis leads to the corresponding Marcus theory rates under the high-temperature and Markovian bath approximations. In addition to including the non-Markovian effect and the low-temperature limits, the theory is also generalized to include the multiple donor-to-acceptor case, as well as including multiple cavity modes. The derivations reveal a comprehensive framework of master equation-based reduced dynamics methods for PMET and other polariton-mediated reactions, providing a promising balance between numeric accuracy and computational efficiency, as well as a step closer to fully scalable simulations of realistic PMET processes.

item.title: Tailored Nitrone [3+2] Dipolar Cycloaddition Enables the Elusive Synthesis of Structurally Complex Seven-Membered Heterocycles
item.description: Intramolecular [3+2] nitrone cycloadditions have seldom been used to construct 7-membered heterocycles as the formation of the competing 6-membered heterocycles is favored almost exclusively. Herein, we report an intramolecular nitrone cycloaddition that proceeds with a strong preference for the formation of seven-membered 2-benzazepines. The reaction tolerates electronically diverse substrates, including heterocyclic variants, delivering a variety of structurally diverse and synthetically challenging 2-benzazepines in yields up to 76% with diastereomeric ratios up to 20:1. DFT calculations provide mechanistic rationale for both the observed regio- and diastereoselectivity and reveal the interplay of the Pauli repulsion and distortion as key selectivity-driving structural effects. The utility of the cycloadducts, especially by exploiting the N−O bond to increase molecular complexity further, is demonstrated through a concise total synthesis of (±)-caulophine A.

item.title: Constructive chemical discovery through autonomous reasoning and experiment
item.description: Making a new reaction often requires chemical knowledge that does not yet exist. Self-driving laboratories and language-model agents now plan, run and optimize experiments rapidly, but deciding what to ask next still requires a chemist in the loop Here we report AIChemist, a robotic chemist for what we call constructive chemical discovery. It decides what to ask next from its own results, settles each question by calculation or experiment, and builds the next design on the answer. Given a silyl-radical-relay concept, AIChemist developed an asymmetric three-component silylcyanation: it established that the solvent effect depended on the oxidant formulation and built the next formulation on this finding, raising the yield from 20% to 67% at 88% enantiomeric excess. For an intermediate of the insecticide broflanilide, it designed a photoredox/nickel C–N coupling route free of nitro-group transformations, at lower estimated cost than the conventional route. When the base favoured by calculation performed poorly, it withdrew that premise and rebuilt the search around the reaction medium, where non-polar toluene raised the product's HPLC yield from 43% to 86%. In both cases, each conclusion extended what the system knew and became the starting point for the next. These results demonstrate a framework for autonomous chemical discovery in which chemical understanding and experimental design evolve together within a closed loop.

item.title: Visible Light Enables NHC–Nickel-Mediated Carbonyl Deletion from Carboxamides
item.description: Electron-rich N-heterocyclic carbene- (NHC-) supported nickel complexes are prized for their reactivity with weak polar functional groups, especially acyl electrophiles. However, synthetic applications leveraging this potent nucleophilicity have been limited to reactivity on the ground-state energy surface, thereby constraining the feasibility of downstream mechanistic steps. Herein, we report the development of a light-driven, NHC-nickel-mediated transformation that takes advantage of the complementary strengths of ground- and excited-state reactivity of NHC-nickel complexes. The carbonyl-deletion protocol enables intramolecular N-arylation from readily accessible carboxamides for the synthesis of di- and triaryl amines under mild conditions (ambient temperatures, additive-free). Combined density functional theory, organonickel intermediate isolation, single-crystal X-ray diffraction, spectroscopy, and radical-probe experiments reveal the origins of substrate-dependent reactivity and the role of light in C–N bond formation. The results support a dinuclear pathway for decarbonylation followed by photoinduced Ni–aryl bond weakening and in-cage C–N-forming radical rebound. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for developing direct photochemical reactivity from electron-rich NHC–nickel complexes relevant to organic synthesis.

item.title: Chiral H2S Ice
item.description: Spontaneous symmetry breaking and the emergence of homochirality have been long-standing mysteries in chemistry and physics. The observation of symmetry breaking in simple triatomic molecules, such as hydrogen sulfide (H2S), is challenging owing to rapid molecular motion and structural relaxation, it provides a fundamental yet poorly understood pathway to molecular handedness in the prebiotic universe.We reportthe firstexperimentalcharacterization of emergent chirality in H2S clusters using vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) in cryogenic matrices (4–40 K). By quenching molecular motion, we resolved a temperature-dependent structural bifurcation: at 10 K, H2S assembles into helical trimer-based strands, characteristic of amorphous ice,whereas at40 K, the system undergoes a cooperative reorganization into crystalline cage-like pentameric networks, characteristic of Phase III crystalline ice. Quantumchemicalsimulationsrevealedthatenthalpiccooperativityinthesethree-dimensional pentameric architectures through S–H⋯S hydrogen bonding and S⋯S interactions provides the criticalstabilizationrequiredforlong-rangecrystallineorder.Kineticanalysesfurther confirmed that the intrinsic chirality of the assemblies remained preserved due to cryogenic trapping, demonstrating the role of directional hydrogen-bonded supramolecular architectures insymmetrybreakingandprovidingexperimentalbenchmarksfortheoreticalmodels developed to treat chirality signatures and prebiotic life in interstellar icy mantles.

item.title: Charged Interface in Battery Breaks Molecular Chiral Symmetry
item.description: Molecular events occurring within a few solvent layers at a charged electrode surface govern the rate and reversibility of reactions in electrochemical devices, yet such interfacial mechanism was never sufficiently understood at atomistic-level. Here we report a counter-intuitive discovery that charged interface breaks down the mirror symmetry between R- and S-enantiomers of propylene carbonate (PC), which expresses at graphite surface into distinct interphasial chemistries. Using enantiopure R- and S-PC as a chemically identical model pair against their racemic mixture, we find interphase at graphite diverges sharply at high lithium salt concentration, where R-PC enables reversible graphite lithiation with a LiF-rich interphase, while S-PC exfoliates graphite. Simulations and spectroscopies identify the combination of high salt concentration and charged interface collectively responsible for inducing the collapse of enantiomerism into diastereomerism. This knowledge not only establishes a hitherto-unknown dimension for electrolyte design, but also introduces a new concept of broad implications beyond battery applications.ed electrode

item.title: Electrolyte-derived interphases control nonuniform charging in battery particle networks
item.description: In an ensemble of battery particles, dynamic interactions among individual particles give rise to emergent behavior like nonuniform charging. Yet, its origins have remained contested due to the challenge of directly measuring the current into each particle. Inspired by neuronal potential recordings in brain-computer interfaces, we present Multichannel Acquisition of Parallel-particle Level Electrochemistry (MAPLE) to map dynamic current distributions in real time. We demonstrate that asynchronous charging in layered oxide cathodes does not originate from bulk properties but instead results from a fluorinated cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI). This CEI forms upon electrolyte exposure before cycling and impedes Li+ transport. Counterintuitively, intergranular cracking rescues these passivated particles by exposing pristine internal surfaces, whereas single-crystal particles without grain boundaries are more vulnerable to this Li+-impeding CEI.

item.title: Framework-Templated Single Clathrate Hydrate Cages in Metal–Organic Frameworks
item.description: Molecular simulations identify metal–organic framework (MOF) pores that retain single methane hydrate cages and, for a nonstandard 16-water cage, support its assembly from disordered water. In smooth spherical pores, a methane molecule assembled twenty waters into the pentagonal dodecahedron of structure I hydrate and sixteen waters into a 435661 cage, a polyhedron that no known hydrate crystal contains. These idealized models were built by language-model agents and then walked back toward real materials, an approach referred to here as agentic doodling, and they guided a screening of 120,419 experimental MOF structures. Most size-matched pores pulled the cage apart, but a small set of frameworks kept it intact at 216 K, better with methane than without, and ELOZIQ kept the dodecahedron up to 270 K, near the melting temperature of the water model. In XODDED and GUQMAH, the nonstandard cage was held at least as well as in an ideal spherical pore, and it self-assembled around methane from randomly placed water, with nearly all of its edges hydrogen bonded. The pores template the cages through a moderate attraction spread over the cage corners rather than through strong binding sites placed at the corners. These results open a route to designing MOFs that hold single hydrate cages, including cages that do not occur in bulk hydrates.

item.title: Anti-Parallel Dimer Structure of p-Cyanophenol Adsorbed at the Aqueous Solution Surface Probed by Sub-1 cm-1 High Resolution
item.description: Sub-1 cm-1 High Resolution Broadband Sum-Frequency Generation Vibrational Spectra (HR-BB-SFG-VS) in different polarization combinations and experimental configurations was used to measure the spectral lineshape in the -CN stretching vibration region of p-cyanophenol (PCP) molecules at the air/water interface. The HR-BB-SFG-VS with a spectral resolution of ~ 0.6 cm-1 provides accurate and nearly intrinsic SFG spectral lineshape with excellent signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). From analyzing the high-resolution spectra in the 2160-2300 cm-1 range, we found that there are two closely overlapping peaks with opposite phases, implying the existence of two -CN groups with opposite orientations at the interface. This finding is unexpected from the conventional perception that PCP molecules at the air/liquid interface forms single Gibbs monolayer at the air/PCP solution interface. In addition, we also found that the -CN spectral intensity dependence on the bulk PCP concentration does not follow the typical Gibbs adsorption layer behavior, that is to follow the Langmuir isotherm, nor follow the anti-parallel double layer adsorption behavior, that is to follow the double-layer adsorption model (DAM) isotherm. By comparing with the -CN signal intensity and lineshape of the 4-(Octyloxy) benzonitrile (C8-PCP) monolayer, as well as orientation analysis of the two opposite peaks with polarization data, we further validated the anti-parallel dimer structure regarding the interfacial configuration of the PCP molecules. These findings not only provided detailed information about the adsorbed organic molecular layers, such as PCP, at the liquid interfaces, but also demonstrated the power of HR-BB-SFG-VS as a uniquely powerful interfacial selective spectroscopy in resolving and discovering detailed and unexpected molecular structure at interfaces.

item.title: Domain-segmented similarity for comparing high-resolution mass spectra of biological samples collected with ambient ionization mass spectrometry
item.description: We introduce a clever domain-segmented mass spectral comparison framework which allows us to incorporate contextual information when comparing high-resolution mass spectra collected with ambient ionization mass spectrometry. We applied this framework when comparing mass spectra of wood samples collected using direct analysis in real-time mass spectrometry, and we found the resulting distribution of similarity scores more naturally follows biological relatedness expectations.

item.title: Processing-and cell-stage thermodynamic screening of nacre-and bone-inspired carbonate and phosphate phases on aluminium current collectors in fluorine-free lithium-ion cells with an open screening framework
item.description: Water-processed, fluorine-free lithium-ion cathodes avoid fluorinated binders and organic solvents, but their alkaline slurry attacks the aluminium current collector, and the cell lacks the protective AlF3 layer that fluorinated salts form. Water-processed (bio-)binders do not protect the collector; the current fixes are pH control with H3PO4 and carbon-coated foil. We ask which nacre- and bone-lineage mineral phases can survive both the alkaline aqueous slurry and the oxidising potential of a fluorine-free cell, and which measurements would decide the rest. We compare nacre-lineage calcium carbonate, bone-lineage calcium phosphates, condensed calcium phosphates and aluminium phosphates as biopolymer-templated coatings, in the slurry (processing stage) and at cell potential (cell stage). Our open, extensible screening framework uses sourced thermochemistry with propagated uncertainty, and reports which phases are excluded, which remain open, and how precise a measurement must be to decide each. Calcite is thermodynamically stable against dissolution at pH 10.0–13.0 for total calcium from 1×10−4 mol dm−3. In a LiClO4-saturated electrolyte, carbonate is thermodynamically excluded above about 4.02 V, and hydroxyapatite and the tricalcium phosphates (upper bounds on oxidation onset 3.98 V–4.07 V) at 4.3 V and above. Condensed calcium phosphates are not excluded at any cutoff-voltage class, and aluminium phosphates are undetermined. Carbonate and bone mineral therefore cannot serve as the cell-stage barrier, and the condensed calcium phosphates remain the open bone-inspired candidates. One slurry-immersion and potential-hold experiment, with two measurements (the Ca2+ transfer free energy into the cell solvent and the template–nucleus interfacial energy), would decide them. No phase can pass the oxidation test while these transfer free energies are unmeasured, and the nucleation model failed its check against literature cases with known outcomes.

item.title: Foldability Is an Intrinsic Property of Protein Sequences: A Lattice Model Study with Information-Theoretic Approach and Unsupervised Machine Learning
item.description: Protein structure prediction has been largely solved, but why a given sequence is foldable has not. We address this question for 27-, 48- and 64-residue lattice heteropolymers with statistical thermodynamics, the informationtheoretic approach (ITA) and a variational autoencoder (VAE). Native populations, folding probabilities and freeenergy surfaces are reproducible and independent of the initial denatured ensemble, so foldability is an intrinsic property of the sequence at a given temperature and solvent. We then ask where the observed regularities come from. Stability is governed by an information balance: the information content (self-information) of the native energy relative to the maximum-entropy description of compact alternatives, ℐtail, must exceed their Shannon entropy, 𝑆c = ln𝛺c. This is the random-energy-model condition for a folding transition, and ℐtail/𝑆c fixes the ratio of folding to glass temperatures, recasting minimal frustration in information units. Foldable sequences have smooth funnels, minimal Shannon entropy and minimal Fisher information in the native state, and a single sharp maximum of Fisher information at melting (cooperativity). Mutual and conditional information show that stability is an approximately sufficient statistic for kinetic accessibility of compact 27-mers. No hierarchical folding order is found. Variational autoencoders trained without labels distinguish sequences by their folding ensembles, supply a six-variable reaction coordinate that retains 91% of the kinetic information in the full native-contact map, and rediscover the native energy gap from the density of compact states.

item.title: Reference Conventions and Structure Types, Rather Than 4f Occupancy, Shape Lanthanide Errors in Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Compounds that pair a lanthanide with a d-block metal and a p-block anion sit behind permanent magnets, catalysts and energy-storage materials, yet large parts of this chemical space have not been computed. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials now make it possible to screen such spaces for stability at a small fraction of the cost of density functional theory, and they are increasingly used to decide which candidates are worth calculating properly. Their training data, however, hold few lanthanide compounds, describe the same element with different pseudopotentials from one database to the next, and carry empirical energy corrections fitted on compound sets from which lanthanides were excluded, so their reliability for felectron chemistry has not been established. Here we benchmark five universal potentials against density functional theory computed with Materials Project settings on 82 lanthanide–d-block–anion ternaries covering the lanthanide series (excluding Pm) and seven anions. Apparent accuracy turns out to be set mainly by the energy convention of the reference: judged against the quantity each model was trained to predict, all five reach mean absolute errors of 0.07 to 0.10 eV per atom, while the wrong convention inflates the error by more than a factor of three. Error does not follow 4f occupancy or the 4f pseudopotential treatment assigned to each element. It is larger for intermetallic than for ionic compounds and concentrates in two structure types, the CeNiC2-type carbides and the PbFCl-type phosphides, which most models miss even though these compounds have Materials Project entries. For ytterbium, every model follows the divalent convention of the older Materials Project data rather than the trivalent one now in use, a singleelement inconsistency of roughly 0.2 to 0.3 eV per atom. These results indicate where lanthanide chemical space can be screened with current potentials and where explicit DFT validation is still required, and they point to structural and data-provenance diagnostics, rather than elemental ones, for the next generation of models.

item.title: A General Cobalt-Catalyzed Oxidative Radical-Polar Crossover Platform for Secondary and Primary Alkyl Radicals
item.description: Along with recent advances in photoredox-mediated radical generation, oxidative radical–polar crossover (ORPC), involving single-electron oxidation of an alkyl radical to the corresponding carbocation, has emerged as a promising strategy for carbocation generation without use of strong acid mediators. However, current photoredox-mediated ORPC systems are not applicable to secondary and primary alkyl radicals due to their short lifetimes and high oxidation potentials, thereby hampering the development of general synthetic platforms for radical/cation-mediated alkylation of heteroatom nucleophiles and rearrangement reactions. Herein, we develop a cobalt-catalyzed ORPC system for secondary or primary alkyl radicals. It involves the radical capture of an alkyl radical by a cobalt(II) complex followed by oxidation of the resultant alkyl cobalt(III) complex to the alkyl cobalt(IV) complex, which participates in an SN2 reaction with heteroatom nucleophiles or rearrangement reactions. Following this strategy, we design a triple photoredox/cobalt/Brønsted acid catalysis and apply it to secondary or primary alkylation of heteroatom nucleophiles. The cobalt-mediated ORPC system could merge with various radical processes, such as b-cleavage and radical addition, which dramatically enables to expand accessible structures.

item.title: Probing ionomer distribution in PEMFC catalyst layers: AFM and DEM enabled microstructure analysis
item.description: Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) catalyst layers have been probed experimentally and theoretically for decades. However, existing microscopy techniques lack the ability to perform quantitative analyses on the catalyst and ionomer distributions of catalyst layers. Since the microstructure of the catalyst layer has an influence on the electrochemical performance, the simulation of catalyst layer microstructures is of great importance. A physics-based simulation model was recently reported to predict the microstructure of the catalyst layer as a function of ink composition. We propose a workflow to characterize catalyst layers with the utilisation of Atomic Force Microscopy. The novelty of the workflow lies in the calculation of a statistical description of the catalyst layer (CL). This statistical metric is then used as a validation metric for a microstructural physics-based simulation model. The resulting simulation workflow can be used to predict the ink composition required to obtain catalyst layers with desired microstructural properties, paving the way towards more efficient PEMFCs.

item.title: A General Approach for the Generation of alpha-Thioalkyl Radicals from Pinacol Boronic Ester Precursors
item.description: A straightforward and effective method to produce alpha-thioalkyl radicals using stable and readily accessible pinacol boronic ester precursors is described. The generation of alpha-thioalkyl radicals proceeds via in-situ transesterification with MeOBcat or 3-methoxycatechol (MOC), and subsequent nucleohomolytic substitution at the boron atom with an oxygen-centred radical. The alpha-thioalkyl radicals can be trapped intermolecularly using a variety of conjugated enones and sulfonyl-based radical traps or subjected to intramolecular cyclisation.

item.title: Selective Adsorption Processes in Mordenite-Catalysed Ethanol Dehydration
item.description: Ethanol dehydration offers a promising solution to improve the sustainability of ethene production, using biomass-derived feedstocks and a heavy-metal-free zeolite catalyst. To improve understanding of the key chemical steps in this reaction, the adsorption of key species in acid-catalysed ethanol dehydration have been investigated on Brønsted Acid (BA) sites in protonated mordenite (MOR). The strength of the BA sites has been characterised using adsorption enthalpies of NH3, revealing that the proximity of the zeolite framework at each BA site is important for stabilisation through van der Waals interactions. Ethanol is found to adsorb more exothermically to the BA sites than the reaction products of ethene and H2O, suggesting that reactant adsorption is not thermodynamically hindered. Reaction selectivity can be tuned by introduction of pyridine. Calculated pyridine adsorption enthalpies indicate that pyridine preferentially occupies specific BA sites, thereby influencing the distribution of active sites available for reaction. In particular, pyridine binds significantly stronger at 12-membered-ring BA sites, which are associated with lower ethene selectivity, than to the more selective 8-membered-ring side pocket BA sites. The results of this paper show that additives may increase reaction selectivity by controlling access to different BA sites, highlighting a potential strategy for improving the performance and versatility of zeolite catalysts.

item.title: DFT Studies of Coherent States in Triphenylamine Trimers
item.description: Density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) calculations were performed to investigate the degree of coherence in two triphenylamine trimers: restricted and unrestricted. The B3LYP/6-31+G(d,p) level of theory was employed in this study. Toluene and dichloromethane were used as solvents to understand the effects of the solvent environment on the properties of the trimers. The unrestricted trimer exhibits a larger HOMO-LUMO energy gap and a shorter absorption wavelength than the restricted trimer, indicating a lower degree of coherence. The solvent effects on the HOMO-LUMO energy gap and UV-Vis absorption spectra are minimal, whereas the intensities of the IR absorption peaks are affected more significantly.

item.title: Synthesis of zigzag-type carbocationic nanobelts
item.description: Belt[n]arenes correspond the shortest belt segments of zigzag carbon nanotubes. Their closed cyclic π-conjugated topologies and distinct size-dependent electronic configurations render them platforms for the construction of quantum materials and devices. Here, we report the synthesis of a fully conjugated carbocationic zigzag-type belt consisting of four linearly fused benzotropylium units. Belt[4]arene[4]tropylium salt was synthesized from resorcin[4]arene via a sequence featuring fjord-stitching olefin metathesis reactions, selective bromination and heterolytic C–Br bond cleavage reaction. Single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis confirms that the synthesized molecule is a rigid C4v-symmetric belt with all positively charged seven-membered rings adopting a boat conformation. Combined evidence from 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, electronic absorption spectra, single crystal structural characterization and theoretical calculations demonstrates the global aromatic nature of belt[4]arene[4]tropylium.

item.title: Can existing or future pathways reduce green ammonia production costs?
item.description: Many scenarios for the energy transition consider green ammonia. The technologically most mature production process combines water electrolysis and Haber-Bosch process (EHB). Its costs are dominated by electrolyzer investment costs and electricity. Emerging pathways researched in academia, start-ups, and industry try to reduce costs by changing sub-processes and chemistry. However, it remains unclear which pathways have the potential to outperform EHB, if any. We assess relevant emerging pathways, compare to EHB in terms of costs and energy demand, and derive performance targets. Many pathways investigated in the literature, such as metalmediated electrolysis, have theoretical minimal energy demands well above the actual energy demand of EHB; consequently, they cannot produce ammonia at competitive costs due to the high influence of electricity costs. Any novel pathway must employ simple and energy-effective chemistry to substantially reduce costs. Identified performance targets are applicable to novel pathways and can guide research, industry, and policy makers.

item.title: Adsorption of cations at electrochemical interfaces revisited
item.description: At electrochemical interfaces, alkali-metal and alkaline-earth metal cations are usually described as solvated species that nonspecifically adsorb, whereas specifically adsorbed anions interact more directly with metal electrodes. However, the mode of cation-surface interaction remains poorly defined at the atomic scale because experiments typically measure averaged interfacial responses. Distinguishing hydration modulated polarization from localized ion-surface coupling therefore requires access to both the atomic structure and the redistribution of electronic charge. Using density functional theory molecular dynamics, we reexamine this distinction for hydrated K+, Na+, Ca2+, oand Mg2+ at Pt(111), Au(111), and Ag(111) metal-water interfaces. Charge neutral, symmetric 3 × 3 cells containing one cation and five to seven water molecules at each interface allow for the study of compact, ion-rich layer configurations, rather than dilute electrolytes or electrodes maintained at an applied potential. Within the sampled compact layer configurations, structural sampling and charge density difference analysis indicate that cation adsorption spans a continuum of interfacial responses, ranging from diffuse, hydration modulated polarization to localized, compact layer coupling. Divalent cations exhibit the most persistent direct contact, and the selected divalent configurations show localized electronic redistribution, while monovalent cations are more sensitive to water coverage and substrate identity. Even predominantly non-contact cations can remain electronically relevant by polarizing the interfacial water layer and metal surface. These results suggest that cation adsorption within the compact interfacial region requires a local, structure dependent description that goes beyond simple specific or nonspecific classifications.

item.title: A New Perspective in Chemical Probe Discovery: Expanding Virtual Screening into Metal Complex Chemical Space
item.description: Transition metal complexes provide rigid, shape-defined molecular architectures in which the coordination geometry precisely organizes ligand functionality in three dimensions, making them attractive scaffolds for target-based chemical probe discovery. Yet, their broader and prospective use in structure-based virtual screening has remained largely unexplored, due to the absence of structurally diverse, computationally tractable screening libraries. Here, we address this by curating MOSAIC (Metal complex library for Structure-Aided In silico screening), a first collection of 16,901 neutral, drug-like metal complexes assembled directly from experimentally determined geometries deposited in the Cambridge Structural Database. Using MOSAIC, we perform a high-throughput virtual screening campaign against the allosteric pocket of methionine adenosyltransferase 2A (MAT2A), identifying the copper complex Cu1-Complex, for which nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF) confirmed strong binding in vitro. The diamagnetic zinc analogue Zn1-Complex allowed orthogonal binding characterization with ligand-observed and competition NMR studies. Along with Hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), site-directed mutagenesis and molecular dynamics (MD), these studies show that Zn1-Complex engages the MAT2A through an allosteric pocket, inhibiting enzymatic activity. Together, this establishes MOSAIC as a scalable and generalizable virtual screening platform for transition metal complexes and demonstrates the potential of these metal-based scaffolds as chemical probes to uncover new modes of protein recognition.

item.title: New Oxygen Sensor with Polyaniline Spin Probe and Low Frequency EPR (L-Band) Detection System
item.description: Our research demonstrates the potential of certain PANI samples to serve as sensitive and reliable spin probes for oxygen detection, while also highlighting the advantages of the lowfrequency EPR technique. Compared to other methods of measuring oxygen concentration, the new sensor—based on a PANI spin probe and a low-frequency EPR detector—offers unique benefits: it ensures high sensitivity to changes in oxygen concentration and does not require direct contact between the EPR detector and the sensor itself (the polyaniline probe). This sensor can be placed in isolated environments, including biological samples (tissues), and - thanks to the use of nanodispersed polyaniline - even inside living cells.

item.title: Overcoming Sensitivity Barrier in 13C NMR Using Frequency–Time Dual-Domain GANs: Quantitative Reaction Monitoring at Natural Abundance
item.description: Low sensitivity has long limited the use of heteronuclei such as 13C and 15N NMR for quantitative chemical measurements, confining reaction monitoring largely to proton-detected experiments. Although highly sensitive, proton NMR often becomes unreliable due to severe signal overlap. Here we show that machine-learning-enabled heteronuclear NMR overcomes this limitation, enabling accurate, time-resolved reaction monitoring using natural-abundance 13C nuclei without isotopic enrichment or hardware modification. We introduce a frequency–time dual-domain generative adversarial network that enforces physical consistency between the free-induction decay and its frequency-domain spectrum. This dual-domain constraint suppresses noise while preserving peak intensities and lineshapes essential for quantitative analysis. We demonstrate that baseline-based signal-to-noise ratios become unreliable after ML-assisted denoising due to non-uniform noise floors, and therefore adopt a true signal-to-noise ratio based on peak-area variance. Using this metric, our approach achieves a two- to three-fold improvement in quantitative sensitivity, comparable to detection using cryogenically cooled probe-heads. Applied to the acid-catalysed inversion of sucrose, the method enables reliable 13C-based kinetic analysis with sub-minute acquisition times per spectrum, establishing a general framework for extending quantitative reaction monitoring beyond proton NMR.

item.title: The Oxidation of Drug Molecules Using the Peroxygenase Activity of a Bacterial Family of Cytochrome P450 Enzymes
item.description: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes with peroxygenase activity can use H2O2 as the sole oxidant which is beneficial for biocatalytic applications. We investigated the peroxygenase activity of CYP105D18 from Streptomyces laurentii. The modification of the acid-alcohol pair in the I-helix through protein engineering reduced the peroxygenase activity for papaverine oxidation by 6-fold compared to the wild-type (WT) enzyme. We identified the oxidation metabolites as papaverine N-oxide, and two newly identified metabolites that arise from O-demethylation. The major O-demethylation metabolite was characterized as 6-O-desmethyl papaverine. Given the higher peroxygenase activity of the unmodified CYP105D18 enzyme we explored if another enzyme from the same CYP subfamily had similar activity. We produced and purified CYP105D41 from Streptomyces thermoviolaceus and found that this enzyme also has significant peroxygenase activity. CYP105D41 could catalyze the oxidation of papaverine and diclofenac. For this enzyme the oxidation of diclofenac was the more efficient reaction and generated 4′-hydroxydiclofenac, 5-hydroxydiclofenac and a doubly hydroxylated metabolite. Overall, we demonstrate that two CYP105 enzymes are effective natural peroxygenase biocatalysts and could efficiently oxidize drug molecules to generate human drug metabolites. These drug molecules are also emerging contaminants, and their oxidation would facilitate their removal from or breakdown in the environment.

item.title: A Non-equilibrium Statistical Mechanics-Based Diffusion Theory: A Unified Model for Diffusion in Porous Media (II)
item.description: Starting from the linear response theory of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, this study establishes a unified model that comprehensively describes bulk diffusion, Knudsen diffusion, and interface diffusion. The diffusion process within porous media is decoupled into a bulk–Knudsen diffusion process and an interface diffusion process, and the flux expressions corresponding to each process are derived separately. The influence of the geometric structure and physicochemical properties of porous media on the Onsager phenomenological coefficients is analyzed, and the variation of the ratio of the chemical potential gradient to the concentration gradient is revealed. On this basis, the ratio of interface diffusion to bulk–Knudsen diffusion is derived and proposed as a criterion for the transition of diffusion mechanisms. The influence of the geometric structure and physicochemical properties of porous media on this criterion is further discussed. Finally, the relationships between this model and the classical theories are analyzed. The proposed model captures the constitutive relationship between the geometric structure and physicochemical properties of porous media and their diffusion capacity, providing a new theoretical paradigm for the construction of diffusion models in porous media.

item.title: Accelerating characterization of conformational stability for biologics in Discovery space by combining SEC‑HDX‑MS with molecular modeling
item.description: Conformational stability is a critical attribute for biologics discovery and manufacturability assessment, yet conventional approaches often require substantial material, extensive preparation, or lack sufficient structural resolution for early decision-making. Here, we present a native size-exclusion chromatography hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (SEC-HDX-MS) workflow integrated with molecular modeling to rapidly characterize conformational stability of therapeutic proteins in the discovery space. The workflow was evaluated across monoclonal antibody and bispecific antibody modalities. From a sequence variant comparison, SEC-HDX-MS showed that elevated aggregation did not uniformly reflect global conformational instability; instead, only one variant displayed increased deuterium incorporation, which modeling linked to an elongated, solvent-exposed CDR-H3 loop with increased hydrophobicity. In a representative proprietary mAb (“mAb X”), SEC-HDX-MS revealed that thermally-induced isoaspartate accumulation reduced conformational stability, whereas high-pH stress showed behavior comparable to controls despite higher overall deamidation. Molecular dynamics simulations explained this destabilization through disruption of a backbone Asn43–Ala40 hydrogen bond and altered local coordination after isoAsp formation. Finally, application to a complex bispecific antibody confirmed the workflow’s sensitivity for detecting conformational differences in more complex formats. Collectively, this integrated approach connects global HDX measurements with molecular-level interpretation, requires minimal preparation and limited material, and is compatible with partially purified samples. The workflow enables rapid conformational stability assessment to support candidate ranking, protein engineering, formulation development, and CMC risk assessment during biologics discovery.

item.title: Partial Pressure Modulation as a Method to Access Non-Equilibrium States in Heterogeneous Catalysis
item.description: Under steady-state conditions, heterogeneous catalyst surfaces are often represented by thermodynamically favoured surface configurations defined by temperature and pressure. However, catalyst surfaces are inherently dynamic and can populate non-equilibrium states that differ from those expected based on the reaction environment. Herein, we show how partial pressure modulation can be utilised to sustain access to non-equilibrium states. Using CO oxidation over Pd/Al2O3 as a model system, we demonstrate how oscillating the partial pressures of CO and O2 drives the catalyst surface into a non-equilibrium state, accessing CO* coverages and reactivities unattainable under steady-state conditions. We find that accessing this state enhances catalytic rate up to three times above the steady-state maximum at a given temperature and induces activity under conditions where no steady-state activity can be recorded. Numerical simulations reproduce similar rate enhancements, demonstrating that accessing non-equilibrium states via dynamic operation can enhance activity without invoking catalyst reconstruction or alternative kinetic pathways. We conclude that the rate enhancement is directly related to disrupting the thermodynamically expected relationship between the gas and surface concentrations. More broadly, these findings suggest that dynamic reactor operation provides a powerful strategy for accessing non-equilibrium states and revealing otherwise inaccessible catalytic behaviour.

item.title: Correcting the Liquid Densities of Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Using Local-Number-Density Repulsion
item.description: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) such as UMA, trained on reference data from meta-generalized gradient approximation or hybrid functionals that incorporate dispersion interactions, often overestimate molecular-liquid densities, thereby placing every property computed at constant pressure at the wrong state point. This study proposes a correction that adds to the MLIP a repulsive energy quadratic in the local number density of each atom, with two coefficients fitted only to the equations of state of water and ethanol; the forces and stresses follow analytically, so neither electronic-structure calculations nor retraining is required. For UMA, the correction reduces the density mean absolute error (MAE) of 22 liquids from 10.8% to 2.5%, lowering the error for every liquid and bringing 20 of them within ±5% of experiment, while improving the bulk modulus (MAE from 71.6% to 22.1%), heat of vaporization, and second hydration shell of water, none of which was calibrated. Applied to SevenNet-Omni without recalibration, the same coefficients reduce the density MAE from 8.2% to 1.8%, with 21 of 22 liquids within ±5% of experiment.

item.title: Hybrid Joining Technologies for Composites: Mechanisms, Performance, Challenges, and Perspectives
item.description: Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites are increasingly used in aircraft structures with their high specific strength, stiffness, corrosion resistance, and lightweight nature. However, reliably joining FRP components is challenging because mechanical joining can create stress concentrations, fiber damage, and delamination, while adhesive bonding can cause peel stress, environmental degradation, and inspection challenges. This review systematically covers hybrid joining approaches for FRPs, emphasizing joint designs, load-sharing mechanisms, mechanical performance, surface treatment, interlayer engineering, aerospace applications, certification concerns, and emerging technologies. This systematic literature review focused on bolted-bonded, riveted-bonded, welded-bonded, and friction-based hybrid connections. The review analyzed the evaluated research for static strength, fatigue behavior, impact resistance, failure mechanisms, joint design parameters, surface modification, interlayer engineering, aerospace implementation, inspection, repair, and certification. Other emerging themes included structural health monitoring, thermoplastic composites, automated joining, and bio-inspired interfaces. Based on the literature, this study shows that hybrid joining provides load-transfer mechanisms and progressive failure behavior comparable to those of single-joining approaches. Reported impact testing suggests that hybrid joints absorb roughly 45% more energy than adhesive joints. Moreover, surface treatments such as abrasion, plasma treatment, laser ablation, and chemical etching, as well as toughening interlayers, can further improve interfacial performance and damage tolerance. Aircraft applications include thermoplastic control surface components, wing-box joints, and fuselage splices. The performance of hybrid FRP joints depends heavily on controlled load sharing between the adhesive and mechanical or friction-based joints. Therefore, adhesive layer thickness, fastener torque, edge distance, overlap length, and fastener spacing are important in reducing stress concentrations and progressive failure. Tailored interlayers and surface activation may further improve fracture resistance and adhesion. However, the following are restricted: certification, non-destructive assessment, long-term durability, repair techniques, and uniformity of repair procedures. Future work should develop new solutions for monitoring, automation, production efficiency, and damage tolerance by combining embedded sensors, machine learning, thermoplastic welding, robotic joining, and bio-inspired interfaces. Hybrid joining methods provide an integrated approach to enhancing the structural performance of FRP composite connections, including damage tolerance, fatigue endurance, and reliability, particularly in aerospace applications. This is achieved through complementary joining techniques that enable gradual load transfer and maintain load-carrying capacity after local damage. Future research should also focus on standardized qualification procedures, standardized processes for reliable non-destructive inspection, environmental durability, automated process control, intelligent health monitoring, and scalable certification procedures to enable the wider application of hybrid composite joining technologies in next-generation aerospace structures.

item.title: Sustainable Surface Metallurgy for Public Health: A Review of Barrier Degradation, Structural Heterogeneity, and Aluminum Leaching Dynamics in Low-Income Country Cookware
item.description: Aluminum (Al) consumer cookware remains a cornerstone of global food preparation due to its exceptional thermal efficiency and low cost. However, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), the widespread reliance on low-purity, informally recycled artisanal alloys creates severe public health risks due to heavy metal migration into dietary pathways. This review explicitly links materials engineering for sustainable development with global safety frameworks by evaluating surface modification technologies designed to mitigate aluminum ion leaching under aggressive thermal and chemical cooking conditions. This review systematically synthesizes the thermodynamic, kinetic, and mechanical performance of three dominant protective systems: electrochemical anodization, sol-gel quasi-ceramic matrices, and fluoropolymer barriers. The chemical stability of these systems is analyzed using mass transport models, chelation-assisted coordination mechanics, and the Arrhenius activation energy framework. Furthermore, a sequential technical characterization workflow is established—linking Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM-EDX), X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS)—to evaluate barrier performance against the strict specific migration limits (SML) enforced by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). While hard anodization and ceramic coatings offer excellent thermal stability, their long-term barrier performance is often compromised by interfacial shear stresses driven by mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) and mechanical wear. This issue is particularly severe in informal metallurgical sectors. Artisanal castings feature high structural porosity and iron/copper micro-impurities that create localized galvanic micro-cells (Δ E > 1.0 V), accelerating the breakdown of surface oxide barriers and leading to heavy metal migration that routinely exceeds international safety standards by factors of 10 to 50. Critical commercial research gaps are identified, specifically the development of cost-effective, bio-based non-stick barriers (e.g., cross-linked green nanocomposites) and the implementation of decentralized circular economy scrap-sorting upgrades. Resolving these material vulnerabilities is essential for advancing UN Sustainable Development Goals related to good health and well-being (SDG 3), clean manufacturing (SDG 9), and responsible consumption and production (SDG 12). This work provides a clear roadmap for scalable, non-hazardous cookware manufacturing tailored for vulnerable populations.

item.title: Physicochemical and Structural Determinants of BACE1-Selective Inhibition: An Integrative Modeling Study using A Combined Ligand-and Structure-Based Approach
Mitigating Catalyst Leaching and Deactivation in Heterogeneous Hydrogen-Bonding/Tertiary Amine Chiral Organocatalysts
item.description: The heterogenisation of chiral organocatalysts remains a key strategy for developing sustainable and recyclable chemical processes. However, long-term stability is often compromised by catalyst leaching and deactivation. In this work, we present a combined computational and experimental study of the deactivation pathways in an ester-linked heterogeneous thiourea/tertiary amine organocatalyst. By identifying the fundamental causes of activity loss, we establish a rational design framework for developing a more robust, high-performance triazole-linked heterogeneous catalyst with extended lifetime and improved reusability.

item.title: Heavy Metal-Binding Peptide Phytochelatin Drives Membraneless Compartmentalization and Biomineral-Like Structures via Nanoparticle Formation within Condensates
item.description: Phytochelatin is a heavy metal-binding biogenic peptide found across different organisms that helps cells mitigate cytotoxicity by chelating metal ions. Yeasts produce phytochelatin to chelate intracellular cadmium and sequester it as cadmium metal sulfide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles were proposed to be stored within cytoplasmic microcompartments, although it remains unclear whether they are stored within membrane-bound or membraneless compartments. Here, we focused on the structure of phytochelatin and hypothesized that it can form membraneless compartments with positively charged biomolecules, which are capable of internal cadmium sulfide sequestration. Indeed, mixing phytochelatin with natural polysaccharide chitosan led to the instant formation of membraneless condensates. Moreover, Cd and S were preferentially accumulated within the condensates relative to other elements and CdS nanoparticles formed inside them. These nanoparticles exhibited crystalline features, with sizes of 2–3 nm and structures comparable to those of the CdS particles observed in cells, which predominantly correspond to the hawleyite structure. This study demonstrated that heavy metal-binding peptides can participate in the formation of membraneless compartments and internal sequestration of nanoparticles. Our findings further indicate a potential role of phytochelatin-based membraneless compartments in spatially controlled intracellular biomineralization and heavy metal sequestration for cellular detoxification, which remains to be explored in vivo.

item.title: Portfolio Search with Precedent-Based Selection for Multi-Step Retrosynthesis
item.description: Computer-aided synthesis planners propose routes from a target molecule back to purchasable starting materials, and they are usually compared by how often they find such a route. A route that reaches purchasable stock, however, often contains steps that have no precedent in the chemical literature and that a chemist would not run. We present P*, a planner that searches with a portfolio of complementary strategies and then keeps, for each target, the route whose every step has literature precedent. Each strategy pairs a reaction score with an estimate of how hard an intermediate is to make. The reaction scores are built from chemical heuristics, such as how common a transformation is and how many of its precursors are purchasable. We find that the strategies that reach stock most often produce the fewest precedented routes, because rewarding purchasable precursors favors multicomponent disconnections that are rarely reported. Different strategies therefore find different precedented routes, and together they find precedented routes for about twice as many development targets as the best single strategy. P* produces fully precedented routes for 61% of approved drugs and clinical candidates, 41% of novel expert-curated targets and 49% of USPTO-190 targets, more than any published planner on all three sets. It exceeds the strongest of them, and it improves route validity with every single-step model we tested. Its best single strategy is also an effective route finder and solves 88.0% of ChEMBL-1000 targets.

item.title: Model-Kernel Corrected DIIS: Cheap Response Information for the Roothaan Step
item.description: Nearly all Kohn–Sham density functional theory (DFT) and Hartree–Fock calculations solve the self-consistent field (SCF) equations with the direct inversion in the iterative subspace (DIIS). Their cost is set by the number of Fock builds that DIIS needs. Each DIIS cycle diagonalizes an extrapolated Fock matrix as if this matrix stayed fixed while the electrons move. The charge that the step moves, however, changes the Coulomb potential, and the next cycle has to undo part of the step. This charge sloshing makes DIIS slower as molecules grow. We correct every step with a model kernel, an inexpensive approximation of this Coulomb response that is built from a few Gaussian functions on each atom and contains no fitted parameters. The resulting method, MK-DIIS, needs no extra Fock build, converges to the same solution as DIIS and adds about 1% to the run time. On 170 transition-metal complexes and organic molecules it needs about one third fewer Fock builds than DIIS, fewer than any SCF algorithm of a production code that we compared with. On molecules with up to 300 atoms it needs about half as many, and on linear acenes its number of Fock builds does not grow with length. The saving is smaller with more exact exchange and in a continuum solvent, both of which screen the Coulomb response. For open-shell molecules, a delayed start keeps the reliability of DIIS. Because only the diagonalization step changes, the correction can be added to existing SCF codes and combined with other convergence aids.

item.title: Removal of Cu(II) and a PET Glitter Microplastic Surrogate by Alginate, Alginate–Opuntia, and Chitosan-Treated Alginate–Opuntia Beads
item.description: The use of alginate-only beads, alginate–Opuntia (AO) beads, and chitosan-treated AO beads for the removal of Cu(II) and a PET glitter (a microplastic surrogate) from water has been investigated. Each bead type was made from the previous one by the addition of one component. Batch experiments were carried out in water containing glitter, Cu(II), or both, and AO beads soaked in dilute acetic acid without chitosan served as a control for the acid. The removal of Cu(II) in copper-only water was 45.71 ± 1.97%, 59.44 ± 2.28%, and 84.19 ± 2.65% for the alginate-only, AO, and chitosan-treated beads, respectively (mean ± SD, n = 12, 6 h, 140 rpm). Opuntia increased the Cu(II) removal by 13.72 percentage points and chitosan by a further 24.75 points (paired t-test, p < 0.001 for both, and p ≤ 0.0013 for the batch means). In the presence of 2.00 g of glitter, the chitosan-treated beads still removed about 84% of the Cu(II). Meanwhile, the glitter removal increased by about 7 points with Opuntia but changed by less than 0.25 points with chitosan (p = 0.648 and 0.231). No significant difference was found between the acid-soaked and the untreated AO beads. It can be concluded that Opuntia was responsible for the increase in glitter capture and chitosan for most of the increase in Cu(II) removal.
